desc:
Given a binary tree, return its values grouped by level. The result is a list of lists: the first list holds the root, the second list holds the children of the root, and so on. Inside every list the values go from left to right. The empty tree gives [].

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [3, 9, 20, -1, -1, 15, 7] the answer is [[3], [9, 20], [15, 7]].
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: The array is already in level order. The only job is to find where one level ends and the next one begins.
A node is on the level right below its parent. Walk the nodes in array order and give each child the level of its parent plus one.
Keep a depth value per real node. When you reach a node, append its value to result[depth], creating a new inner list the first time that depth appears.
editorial: The classic way is a breadth-first search with a queue: process the queue one whole level at a time by taking the current size of the queue, popping that many nodes, and pushing their children for the next round.

With this array encoding no queue is needed. The real nodes appear in level order, so parents always come before their children. A single left-to-right pass can set depth[child] = depth[parent] + 1 and append every node to the list of its depth. Every node is handled once, so the time is O(n).
